content: This is an updated version of a Cochrane Review, originally published in 2014 and last updated in 2020. Approximately 30% of individuals with epilepsy experience drug-resistant seizures that are not adequately controlled by current treatments. Stiripentol is an antiepileptic drug (AED) developed in France and approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2007 as an adjunctive therapy, specifically in combination with valproate and clobazam, for the treatment of Dravet syndrome. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of stiripentol as an add-on treatment for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy who are already receiving AEDs. For the most recent update, a search was conducted on March 28, 2022, using the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE. Additionally, the manufacturer of stiripentol and epilepsy experts were contacted to identify any published, unpublished, or ongoing trials. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the use of stiripentol as an add-on therapy in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The outcomes assessed included a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, complete seizure freedom, adverse effects, treatment withdrawal, and changes in quality of life. No new studies were identified for inclusion in this updated review. Only one study from the original review met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 32 children with focal epilepsy and used a responder-enriched design. The findings did not provide clear evidence that stiripentol, when used as an add-on therapy, resulted in a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 1.51, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.81 to 2.82; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, there was no clear evidence of seizure freedom with stiripentol compared to placebo (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.31 to 4.43; low-certainty evidence). The study indicated that stiripentol was associated with a higher risk of adverse effects overall compared to placebo (RR 2.65, 95% CI 1.08 to 6.47; low-certainty evidence). However, when specific adverse effects were analyzed, the confidence intervals were wide, suggesting the possibility of both significant increases and small reductions in the risk of neurological adverse effects (RR 2.65, 95% CI 0.88 to 8.01; low-certainty evidence). There was no clear reduction in the risk of treatment withdrawal with stiripentol compared to placebo (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.47; low-certainty evidence). Notably, the withdrawal rates were high in both groups, with 53.3% in the placebo group and 35.3% in the stiripentol group (low-certainty evidence). The external validity of the study was limited because only participants who responded to stiripentol during an open pre-randomization phase (defined as a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to baseline) were included in the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase. Additionally, carry-over and withdrawal effects likely influenced the outcomes related to seizure frequency. The limited data from this single study suggest that adverse effects may occur more frequently with add-on stiripentol than with placebo. However, the evidence is of low certainty, and the study design limits the generalizability of the findings. In conclusion, no new studies have been identified since the last version of this review, and the conclusions remain unchanged. There is insufficient evidence to support the use of stiripentol as an add-on treatment for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Further large, randomized, and well-conducted trials are necessary to evaluate the efficacy and safety of stiripentol in this population.
